This section examines Experiment N —
Hybrid restart and precedence

surrogate from first principles. Keep two
questions separate: does changing

the order change the measured outcome, and
does the proposed

search method beat a matched alternative
at the same distinct-evaluation

budget? Landscape highlight: Kendall n=7,
one optimum among 5,040 orderings.

Precedence representation: binary features
indicating whether item i appears

before item j. Audited result reported in
the paper: precedence

surrogate 14.8 [14,15] mean evaluations;
elitist prism 54.2 [50,59]; random

only 2/40 hits within a 500-evaluation
cap. Hybrid restart: retain

best-ever, restart the rest after
stagnation; never the worst in

the studied set but wastes restarts on
some structured landscapes.

Lesson: representation-landscape matching
matters for surrogates just as it

does for mutation. Now read evidence panel
N-surrogate. The axes,

units, and sample are stated on screen.
The sample represented

here is 5,040 orderings. Raw observations
remain visible wherever the

artifact provides them. Censored
observations stay marked at the cap

rather than becoming invented hitting
times, and sampled landscapes leave

unobserved permutations blank. The
supported finding is: Audited result

reported in the paper: precedence
surrogate 14.8 [14,15] mean evaluations;

elitist prism 54.2 [50,59]; random only
2/40 hits within a

500-evaluation cap. The broader claim not
established here is: Audited

result reported in the paper: precedence
surrogate 14.8 [14,15] mean

evaluations; elitist prism 54.2 [50,59];

changed the program as follows:

Carry this constraint into the next
experiment and compare methods

at equal cost. The distinction is part of
the result.

A large ordering effect does not
automatically imply an evolutionary-search

advantage, and almost-sure convergence
does not promise practical
efficiency.
